<pasted_content id="93e7">
*Regressions*

1. *Explain views and --generate point at different checkpoints* (cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:2829). --generate now writes into the last ID of the final trailer block. Plain entire explain --commit X still uses ParseCheckpoint and shows the first ID. On a squash commit with trailers aaaa and bbbb (the PR's own test fixture), the summary goes into bbbb while the view shows aaaa with no summary.

• *Fix:* have the read-only views prefer the final-block ID, and fall back to scanning the whole message only when the final block has none..

2. *The review re-run guard reads a different checkpoint than attach writes* (cmd/entire/cli/head_checkpoint_flags.go:56).

• *Mechanism:* headCheckpointFlags still takes the first Entire-Checkpoint ID anywhere in HEAD's message. Attach now writes into the final-block ID, or adds a new trailer..
• *Effect:* if HEAD has a trailer outside the final block, the review is saved into the new checkpoint B but the guard reads A. It sees HasReview=false, so entire review runs again every time..
• *Fix:* switch to FinalCheckpointTrailers (last ID)..

3. *An emptied git commit -e -m commits only the trailer* (manual_commit_hooks.go:316).

• *Mechanism:* for -e -m, prepare puts the trailer after git's # comment block and doesn't add the explanation text..
• *Effect:* if the user deletes the message and saves, neither of commit-msg's signals is present. The # lines count as content, the trailer is kept, and git records a commit whose whole message is Entire-Checkpoint: <id> instead of aborting..

*Narrower bugs*

4. *core.commentChar=auto still breaks* (manual_commit_hooks.go:2997). This is earlier #3, now reached through commit.cleanup=whitespace. git picks ; because the message has a line starting with #, but the code assumes #. The comment lines then hide the trailer block, so the trailer points to a checkpoint that is never written.

5. *--amend --no-edit and -C <rev> are treated as edited* (manual_commit_hooks.go:2970). git doesn't strip # lines in these cases. A body ending in #42 is mistaken for git's comment block, so the restored trailer is inserted above it and ends up in the middle of the body.

*Cleanup and design*

6. *commit-msg guesses whether the message was edited* (manual_commit_hooks.go:314). It looks at the last line and whether Entire's explanation text is there, even though prepare-commit-msg already knows the commit's source. That guess causes #3.

• *Fix:* record prepare's source the same way the inherited-trailer marker is recorded, and have commit-msg read it..

7. *Repeated git config lookups* (manual_commit_hooks.go:3015). A single squash or redo prepare-commit-msg now runs git config three or more times, some of them before it knows a trailer will be added.

• *Fix:* resolve the comment prefix once per hook and pass it down..

8. *Tests read the developer's real git config* (cmd/entire/cli/attach_test.go:1888). The new cli-package tests reach the git config fallback, but the cli TestMain doesn't isolate git config. Anyone with core.commentChar set globally gets a failing test.

• *Fix:* call testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv..

9. *Confusing error from --generate* (explain.go:2810). When the only Entire-Checkpoint lines sit outside the final block (for example a squash body followed by a Co-authored-by block), it fails with "has no Entire-Checkpoint trailer", even though git log shows one.

• *Fix:* say the commit only mentions checkpoints outside its final trailer block, and name them..

Findings 1–3 should block merge. #1 and #2 are the same root problem: some readers still use ParseCheckpoint while the writers moved to the final block. The fix is to move explain's views and headCheckpointFlags to the same resolver.
</pasted_content id="93e7">

Right, interpret-trailers defaults to "#" for auto mode in config parsing, so the ";" comment lines in the recorded message wouldn't get skipped, meaning the trailer wouldn't land in the final block. I need to check whether the local WIP test around line 220 actually covers this auto+whitespace interaction, since finding 4 suggests it traces back to the earlier auto issue, now reached via commit.cleanup=whitespace.

I should write a quick check to verify this against the local tree before moving on, maybe by examining an editor message with a "# heading" line under auto+whitespace settings. Then for issue 5, involving --amend/-C treated as edited and a body ending in "#42" being mistaken for a trailer block, my new rule seems to correctly avoid a false block when there's no blank line above, but still produces a false positive when there is one, placing the trailer in the middle of the body paragraph.

I'm now wondering if there's a way to distinguish git's generated comment block from user content by its actual content rather than structure -- git's block typically opens with a localized hint line like "Please enter the commit message for your changes," which could be a more reliable signal than relying on --no-edit vs --amend behavior.

That confirms it—git's run_commit_hook sets GIT_EDITOR=":" in the hook's environment when no editor will actually be invoked, so prepare-commit-msg hooks can check that env var to know whether an interactive editor is coming.

This applies to commit-msg too, since "all git commit hooks" includes it—meaning commit-msg could detect editor usage without needing a separate marker. But there's an edge case: if a user intentionally sets GIT_EDITOR=":" to skip editing (common in scripts or CI for auto-accepting merges), git still technically "uses" the editor by invoking it, even though it does nothing—so the hook would see a non-colon GIT_EDITOR value and misclassify this as "edited" when it wasn't really.

The fix is to combine signals: if the comment-stripped block exists at all, that confirms editing happened (since git only writes that block when use_editor is true); if the block is absent and GIT_EDITOR is ":", treat it as not edited; if the block is absent and GIT_EDITOR isn't ":", treat it as edited via the status mechanism. package cli

import (
	"context"
	"os"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint"

	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/paths"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/testutil"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/redact"
	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

const (
	headFlagsTestAuthorName  = "Test"
	headFlagsTestAuthorEmail = "head-flags-test@entire.local"
)

// setupHeadFlagsRepo creates a git repo with an initial commit, switches the
// process CWD to it (cannot t.Parallel — t.Chdir conflicts), and returns the
// opened *git.Repository.
func setupHeadFlagsRepo(t *testing.T) *git.Repository {
	t.Helper()
	tmpDir := t.TempDir()
	testutil.InitRepo(t, tmpDir)
	testutil.WriteFile(t, tmpDir, "init.txt", "init")
	testutil.GitAdd(t, tmpDir, "init.txt")
	testutil.GitCommit(t, tmpDir, "init")
	t.Chdir(tmpDir)
	paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache()

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(tmpDir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	return repo
}

// writeHeadCheckpointWithFlags writes a committed checkpoint and amends
// HEAD so it points at it via the Entire-Checkpoint trailer. The session
// metadata is configured with the supplied flags so the resolved summary
// surfaces them.
func writeHeadCheckpointWithFlags(t *testing.T, repo *git.Repository, hasReview, hasInvestigation bool) id.CheckpointID {
	t.Helper()
	cpID := id.MustCheckpointID("aabbccdd1122")
	store := checkpoint.NewGitStore(repo, checkpoint.DefaultV1Refs())
	require.NoError(t, store.Write(context.Background(), checkpoint.Session{
		CheckpointID:     cpID,
		SessionID:        "head-flags-session",
		Strategy:         "manual-commit",
		Transcript:       redact.AlreadyRedacted([]byte(`{"type":"user","message":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"hi"}]}}` + "\n")),
		AuthorName:       headFlagsTestAuthorName,
		AuthorEmail:      headFlagsTestAuthorEmail,
		HasReview:        hasReview,
		HasInvestigation: hasInvestigation,
	}))

	// Amend HEAD so it carries the Entire-Checkpoint trailer pointing at cpID.
	cwd, err := os.Getwd()
	require.NoError(t, err)
	runGitInDir(t, cwd, "commit", "--amend", "-m", "init\n\nEntire-Checkpoint: "+cpID.String())
	return cpID
}

func TestHeadCheckpointFlags_BothFlagsTrue(t *testing.T) {
	repo := setupHeadFlagsRepo(t)
	cpID := writeHeadCheckpointWithFlags(t, repo, true, true)

	hasReview, hasInvestigation, info := headCheckpointFlags(context.Background())
	require.True(t, hasReview, "HasReview should be true when summary has it set")
	require.True(t, hasInvestigation, "HasInvestigation should be true when summary has it set")
	require.Contains(t, info, cpID.String(), "info string should reference the checkpoint id")
	require.True(t, strings.HasPrefix(info, "checkpoint "), "info should start with 'checkpoint '")
}

func TestHeadCheckpointFlags_NeitherFlag(t *testing.T) {
	repo := setupHeadFlagsRepo(t)
	// Write a checkpoint but with no review/investigate flags, then verify
	// the helper returns (false, false, info) — info is non-empty because a
	// checkpoint exists at HEAD; the flags simply aren't set.
	cpID := writeHeadCheckpointWithFlags(t, repo, false, false)

	hasReview, hasInvestigation, info := headCheckpointFlags(context.Background())
	require.False(t, hasReview)
	require.False(t, hasInvestigation)
	require.Contains(t, info, cpID.String(),
		"info string should still resolve to the checkpoint id even when both flags are false")
}

func TestHeadCheckpointFlags_NoCheckpointAtHead(t *testing.T) {
	// Fresh repo with an initial commit but no Entire-Checkpoint trailer.
	setupHeadFlagsRepo(t)

	hasReview, hasInvestigation, info := headCheckpointFlags(context.Background())
	require.False(t, hasReview)
	require.False(t, hasInvestigation)
	require.Empty(t, info, "info must be empty when HEAD has no Entire-Checkpoint trailer")
}

new='''Prepare reads the message as git will record it. Git tells its commit hooks
whether it opens the editor (`GIT_EDITOR=:` when it does not: `-m`/`-F` without

line down, while any other keeps its comment lines (git's trailer grammar
still skips them), unless `commit.cleanup=strip` drops them from every
message; `whitespace`, `verbatim` and `scissors` keep them in editor messages
too. The prefix is `core.commentChar` or `core.commentString` (aliases; the
last one set wins), `#` when unset, and for `auto` it is read back from the
comment block git wrote into the message, or, with no block to read
(`commit.status=false`, no editor), picked by git's own rule: the first of
`#;@!$%^&|:` that starts no line. Git's comment block is the run of comment
lines after a blank line that ends the message, or the part above the
scissors line (which can also start it); comment lines joined to the
paragraph above them, or a template's own prompts above the block, are the
user's. Every trailer prepare adds to a message git opens goes above that
block, so `commit -v` cannot cut it off; a message git does not open gets its
trailer appended, so its own lines stay in place. The editor template puts
prepare's explanation, written with the same prefix, in its own paragraph
between the user's lines and the trailer: a line typed just above the trailer
cannot join the subject paragraph, and `commit.cleanup` modes that keep comment
lines leave the trailer as its own block. A message git does not open gets no
explanation, which git would keep. Commit-msg judges an emptied message by the
same signal. A recorded commit is read with the configured prefix (`auto`
reads as `#`, as `git interpret-trailers` does). Post-commit also accepts the
one trailer prepare left as the commit's link (stamped, restored, or kept from
the final block) wherever the user's edits moved it (`stampedTrailerFile`,
like the inherited-trailers marker), so pasted text cannot match it; attach
and `explain --generate` still read only the final block, so they see such a
commit as unlinked. The per-commit read-only views (`explain <commit>`,
`explain --commit`, the export, and the review re-run guard) show the
checkpoint attach and `--generate` use (`CommitCheckpoint`), falling back to
the first ID anywhere only when the final block names none. Other read-only
lookups (resume, status, attribution, history listings) and squash and redo
inheritance still scan the whole message, because squash commits carry their
squashed commits' trailers in the body. The trailer writer joins only a block
of trailer lines alone, so a trailer it appends is always one the readers
accept.

'''

`explain --generate`, which takes the block's last ID as attach does).'''

docs/security-and-privacy.md:163:Secret detection as a whole is always on, though the pattern-matching scanner layer within it is configurable per [Choosing secret-scanner engines](#choosing-secret-scanner-engines). Betterleaks pattern matching covers cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), version control platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), payment processors (Stripe, Square), communication tools (Slack, Discord, Twilio), private key blocks (RSA, DSA, EC, PGP, OpenSSH), and generic credentials (bearer tokens, basic auth, JWTs). Dedicated credentialed URI detection covers URLs that embed passwords. Additional database connection-string detection covers DB DSNs and query-parameter passwords not reliably covered by generic secret rules. Entropy scoring catches secrets that don't match any known pattern.

docs/development/checkpoint-implementation.md:61:- **Commit-to-session linking is identity-first** (`strategy/session_identity.go`): identity comes from `SessionState.Owner`, the `proclive.Identity` that `captureSessionOwner` already records on every turn start (first non-transient ancestor — proclive skips shells, `entire` itself, and the Go toolchain, so a human commit typed in the same terminal never matches). Commit hooks snapshot their own ancestry once (`proclive.CurrentAncestry`) and match every candidate against it in memory (`Ancestry.Depth`) — one hostname/boot-id/proc walk per commit, not one per session state — linking the commit to the session whose agent process is an ancestor — in any worktree (nearest ancestor wins, so a nested agent beats the outer agent that spawned it, and only a tie at equal depth falls to the latest interaction; host/boot/start-time guards defeat PID reuse and cross-machine matches; Windows cannot introspect and falls back to worktree matching). The identity match is UNIONED with the worktree-matched set, never a replacement: a commit condenses every session with pending content in its worktree. Any session matched outside its home worktree is guest-linked — whether identity-matched or selected by the pre-existing single-worktree fallback — and is condensed and linked without mutating worktree-coupled state (`BaseCommit`) from the foreign worktree (`isSessionHomeWorktree`). Worktree matching is always computed (it is the sole mechanism for commits with no agent ancestry): imported sessions never link, and multi-worktree ambiguity is filtered to recently-interacting sessions (15 min) before declining. This deliberately turns some former ambiguity declines into a best-candidate link; `recentSessionWindow` is a correctness tradeoff because a session in a long-running build or tool call can age out and leave the other recent worktree to win. **The recency shortcuts trust only the agent's own commit** (`commitProvenance`): the no-TTY / `commit_linking=always` fast path stamps, and PostCommit condenses, ACTIVE and live-task sessions without an overlap check. A session is foreign to a commit when its recorded owner is alive, absent from an ancestry walk that reached init (`Ancestry.Excludes`; a walk cut off by `maxAncestryDepth` or a failed lookup proves nothing), and not named by any agent's caller-session variable; a foreign session skips the fast path, links only on staged-file overlap (task records and transcript growth do not count), and condenses only on committed-file overlap; for an IDLE session a fresh live task whose running subagent wrote a staged or committed file (`liveTaskFilesInCommit`) counts as that overlap. No owner, a dead or unverifiable owner, and Windows keep the shortcuts. # General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.
- Read the Trail's current description and resolved findings before drafting review comments. The trail description can be newer than the PR description and may already list known follow-ups, which turns "you missed this" into a question about scale or timing.
- When a PR claims corpus validation, check what the corpus contained, and test on inputs from outside it, such as other languages and other codebases. A corpus drawn from one codebase can pass while common idioms elsewhere break.
- When a PR adds a second implementation of an existing contract, such as another way to compute an offset or boundary, check it uses the same rule as the existing path and test it with input that hits the contract's edge case. A mock that maps input one-to-one passes whichever rule is used.
- Don't rewrite a value before other detectors scan it; collect detections on the unchanged value and merge them. Masking first can break anchored or overlapping matches and expose text the old pipeline redacted.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

All of A–D and the second review are fixed, folded into local commit `caeefbea7` (the WIP placeholder message is kept; nothing pushed). Of the review's nine items, 3 and 4 were already fixed by the earlier WIP commit, 8 was a false positive, and the rest are fixed.

**What changed**

- **Is git opening the editor?** Git runs commit hooks with `GIT_EDITOR=:` when it won't open the editor (`-m`, `--no-edit`, `-C`); I checked this on git 2.50. Both prepare-commit-msg and commit-msg now use that instead of guessing from the source word or the last line.
  - A message git won't open gets its trailer appended and keeps its lines in place, which settles A, C and review #5.
  - commit-msg judges an emptied message by the same signal, which settles review #6.
- **Finding git's comment block:** it's the run of comment lines after a blank line, at the end of the message or above the scissors line. With `core.commentChar=auto`, the prefix is read back from that block, which fixes B.
- **Stamp marker (D):** it's now recorded when prepare keeps a trailer and on the agent fast path, so a body typed below the trailer no longer blocks post-commit from condensing.
- **Review 1 and 2:** `explain <commit>`, `explain --commit`, the export and the review re-run guard now share one resolver, `strategy.CommitCheckpoint`. It returns the last ID of the final trailer block, which is what `--generate` and attach use. It only falls back to the first ID anywhere when the final block names none.
- **Review 9:** `--generate` now names the checkpoints that sit outside the final block instead of saying the commit has no trailer.
- **Review 7:** prepare-commit-msg reads git's comment config once per hook. I measured with `GIT_TRACE`: the squash and redo tests went from 8 reads to 7, so the saving is one `git config` call per squash or redo commit. That's smaller than the review suggested.
- **Review 8:** no change. The cli package's `TestMain` already isolates git config (`gitenv.IsolateMain()`), including at the reviewed commit, and the tests pass with a global `core.commentChar=S`.

- New tests for each finding all failed before the fix and pass now.
- `mise run check` passed except `TestProbeConfigDir_AsksClaude` (`agent/claudecode`), which timed out at its 5 s limit under full-suite load and passes 3 of 3 alone. This change doesn't touch that package.
- The Vogon canary passes. No real-agent E2E tests were run.

- **F:** attach and `explain --generate` still treat a commit as unlinked when the user moved its trailer out of the final block.
- The explain history listings (`explain.go:1713/1731/2471`) still match a commit by the first ID anywhere.
- If your own `GIT_EDITOR` is `:`, the trailer lands after git's comment block. Git strips the block so the trailer survives, except under `-v`.

**Proposed PR "Known gap" text** (not posted; it needs your approval). Delete the current first paragraph about `git commit -m … -e`, which this round fixes, and add:

> A commit whose stamped trailer the user moves out of the final block in the editor, for example by typing a body below it, is still condensed into that checkpoint: post-commit accepts the trailer prepare left. Attach and `explain --generate` read only the final block, so they treat that commit as unlinked, and `--generate` names the out-of-block checkpoint in its error. Moving the trailer back into the final block would take a new step in commit-msg, so it is left out.

content.text:
Review target: `origin/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block..HEAD`

`xhigh effort → 10 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → sweep → ≤15 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at extra-high effort: catch every real bug. At
this level, catching real bugs matters more than avoiding false positives — a
missed bug ships. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (5 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 8 each)

Run **10 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 8 candidate findings**. Do NOT let one angle's conclusions
suppress another's — if two angles flag the same line for different reasons,
record both.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed

does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

JS falsy-zero, `==` coercion, closure-captured loop var; Python mutable default
args, late-binding closures; Go nil-map write, range-var capture; SQL injection;

adapter): check that every method routes to the wrapped instance and not back
through a registry/session/global — e.g. a caching provider holding a
`delegate` field that resolves IDs via `session.get(...)` instead of

wrapper forwards all the methods the callers actually use.

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,

- **For users:** Entire's commit hooks now write the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer where git will record it in every common `git commit` mode, so it lands in the final trailer block and links the commit. The modes are `-m`, `-m -e`, the editor, `-v`, `--amend`, `--amend --no-edit`, `-C`, templates, and `core.commentChar`/`auto`/`commit.cleanup` configs. The user's own lines stay where they typed them. The per-commit read-only views (`explain <commit>`, `explain --commit`, the export, and the review re-run guard) now show the same checkpoint that `--generate` and attach write.
- **Why:** this PR's security rule (only the final trailer block authorizes checkpoint writes) made trailer placement a correctness requirement. Every mode that left the trailer outside the final block lost its link. Readers that still took the first ID anywhere disagreed with the writers.
- **How:**
  - `GIT_EDITOR=:` (githooks(5)) tells both hooks whether git opens the editor.
  - Git's comment block is the trailing comment run after a blank line, or the scissors line.
  - The `auto` prefix is read back from that block, with a consistency check.
  - The stamp marker is recorded on every path where prepare leaves a link.
  - A per-hook snapshot means one `git config` read per prepare.
  - `strategy.CommitCheckpoint` is the one read-only resolver.
- **Performance:** one `git config` spawn fewer per squash or redo commit (measured: 8 → 7 on those tests). Read-only views add one spawn only when the final block names no ID but the message mentions one.
- **Compatibility:**
  - Messages git doesn't open now always get the trailer appended, so the layout differs from the pushed branch.
  - Squash commits now show their last final-block checkpoint instead of the first.
  - It relies on git's `GIT_EDITOR` contract.

findings.summary: A user- or harness-exported GIT_EDITOR=: is read as 'git does not open the editor', so an untouched editor commit no longer aborts: prepare appends a bare trailer after git's comment block and commit-msg counts git's comment lines as content.
findings.short_summary: Exported GIT_EDITOR=: turns an abort into a trailer-only commit
findings.failure_scenario: Shell or CI exports GIT_EDITOR=: and runs plain `git commit` with an empty message. Git still writes its block and strips comments. Prepare (edited=false) appends the trailer below the block with no explanation. commit-msg (edited=false, default cleanup keeps comments) finds the '# Please enter…' lines and keeps the trailer. Git records a commit whose whole message is `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>`. The pushed branch aborted here via the explanation marker. With -v the trailer also lands below the scissors line and is lost.

findings.summary: preparedFinalTrailers reads the final block with the cleanup prefix (git's auto choice, e.g. ';'), while post-commit, attach and git interpret-trailers read auto as '#'. So under core.commentChar=auto, prepare judges a linked message unlinked.
findings.short_summary: Prepare and post-commit read auto's final block differently
findings.failure_scenario:
core.commentChar=auto, HEAD recorded as 'My change

Entire-Checkpoint: X

#42 is the issue'. On amend git picks ';' because a line starts with '#', so prepare strips ';' lines and sees '#42 is the issue' as the final paragraph. X is not kept, and the restore path appends X a second time. A -F message with its own trailer followed by '#' lines likewise gets a second trailer. Post-commit (reading '#') would have linked the original.

findings.summary: explain's history walks (lines 1713, 1731 and 2471) still match a commit by trailers.ParseCheckpoint's first ID anywhere, so for a squash commit they attribute it to a different checkpoint than CommitCheckpoint, --generate and attach.
findings.short_summary: Explain history listings still use the first ID anywhere
findings.failure_scenario: Squash commit with final block 'Entire-Checkpoint: aaaa\nEntire-Checkpoint: bbbb'. `explain <commit>` now shows bbbb, but the checkpoint listing (collectCheckpoint) attributes the commit to aaaa, and `explain bbbb` finds no commit via the first-parent walk at 1731. This is the same split between reader rules that produced review items 1 and 2.

findings.summary: Post-commit links a commit through the stamp marker when the user moved the trailer out of the final block, but attach, explain --generate and CommitCheckpoint never see the marker. CommitCheckpoint's fallback can then show a different, body-mentioned checkpoint.
findings.short_summary: Marker-linked commit stays unlinked for attach and --generate
findings.failure_scenario: Squash commit where the user typed a body below the stamped trailer Y, and inherited trailer A sits in the body. Post-commit condenses into Y via the marker. `explain --generate` errors that Y is outside the final block, attach stamps yet another trailer, and read-only `explain <commit>` falls back to the first ID anywhere (A), not Y. This is the documented gap F.

findings.summary: Every new placement test drives the hook binary with synthetic messages (gitCommentBlock, gitVerboseTail) and records commits with go-git. The GIT_EDITOR contract, git's real block shape, auto's choice and cleanup are never exercised through real `git commit`, so the tests share the implementation's assumptions.
findings.short_summary: No real-git test of the hook placement contract
findings.failure_scenario: A git version, locale or config that writes its block differently (merge or cherry-pick notes, another hint layout, a status section), or a git mode that sets GIT_EDITOR differently, would pass every test while misplacing the trailer in real use. Earlier review rounds found this class repeatedly. A real-git matrix (modes × configs × message shapes) asserting the final block names the stamped ID, the user's lines are unchanged, and a cleared message aborts would catch it.

findings.summary: Hook-invoking tests that bypass gitHookEnv (here, and antigravity_test.go:328 via prepareCommitMsgCmd) now simulate `git commit -m` as an editor commit, or inherit the developer's GIT_EDITOR, because the hook reads GIT_EDITOR and only the shared helpers set it.
findings.short_summary: Some -m hook simulations inherit or miss GIT_EDITOR
findings.failure_scenario: A developer whose shell exports GIT_EDITOR=: gets different prepare behavior in deferred_finalization_test than CI does. Separately, both tests model -m with the editor flag on, so they stop covering real -m behavior (append, no block, no strip).

findings.summary: The keep paths record different IDs in the stamp marker: the slow and fast paths record stampedTrailer's first non-inherited final-block ID, while the amend keep path (line 855) records the last live one.
findings.short_summary: Keep paths record first vs last ID in the stamp marker
findings.failure_scenario: A -F or template message whose final block holds two non-inherited trailers X, Y: the marker records X. On an amend of the same shape it records Y. If the user then moves one out of the final block, post-commit rescues X in one flow and Y in the other, and pickCondensationTarget's 'last without a checkpoint' rule may pick a different target than the user's intent.

findings.summary: hasUserContent (and preparedFinalTrailers) cut at a scissors line even in a message git does not open, but git cuts only under -v or commit.cleanup=scissors.
findings.short_summary: Scissors cut applied to messages git keeps whole
findings.failure_scenario: `git commit -F saved.txt` where saved.txt is a saved `commit -v` message with its scissors line and diff. Git (no editor, whitespace cleanup) records the diff in the message. Prepare judges the trailer above the scissors line as stamped, but the recorded final block is the diff, so attach and explain see the commit as unlinked. If the content sits only below the scissors line, commit-msg strips the trailer of a message git records non-empty.

findings.failure_scenario: Squash commit with final block 'Entire-Checkpoint: aaaa\nEntire-Checkpoint: bbbb'. `explain <commit>` now shows bbbb, but the checkpoint listing (collectCheckpoint) attributes the commit to aaaa, and `explain bbbb` finds no commit via the first-parent walk at 1731. This is the same split between reader rules that produced review items 1 and 2.

findings.summary: Post-commit links a commit through the stamp marker when the user moved the trailer out of the final block, but attach, explain --generate and CommitCheckpoint never see the marker. CommitCheckpoint's fallback can then show a different, body-mentioned checkpoint.
findings.short_summary: Marker-linked commit unlinked for attach and --generate
findings.failure_scenario: Squash commit where the user typed a body below the stamped trailer Y, and inherited trailer A sits in the body. Post-commit condenses into Y via the marker. `explain --generate` errors that Y is outside the final block, attach stamps yet another trailer, and read-only `explain <commit>` falls back to the first ID anywhere (A), not Y. This is the documented gap F.

findings.summary: Every new placement test drives the hook binary with synthetic messages (gitCommentBlock, gitVerboseTail) and records commits with go-git. The GIT_EDITOR contract, git's real block shape, auto's choice and cleanup are never exercised through real `git commit`, so the tests share the implementation's assumptions.
findings.short_summary: No real-git test of the hook placement contract
findings.failure_scenario: A git version, locale or config that writes its block differently (merge or cherry-pick notes, another hint layout, a status section), or a git mode that sets GIT_EDITOR differently, would pass every test while misplacing the trailer in real use. Earlier review rounds found this class repeatedly. A real-git matrix (modes × configs × message shapes) asserting the final block names the stamped ID, the user's lines are unchanged, and a cleared message aborts would catch it.

findings.summary: Hook-invoking tests that bypass gitHookEnv (here, and antigravity_test.go:328 via prepareCommitMsgCmd) now simulate `git commit -m` as an editor commit, or inherit the developer's GIT_EDITOR, because the hook reads GIT_EDITOR and only the shared helpers set it.
findings.short_summary: Some -m hook simulations inherit or miss GIT_EDITOR
findings.failure_scenario: A developer whose shell exports GIT_EDITOR=: gets different prepare behavior in deferred_finalization_test than CI does. Separately, both tests model -m with the editor flag on, so they stop covering real -m behavior (append, no block, no strip).

findings.summary: The keep paths record different IDs in the stamp marker: the slow and fast paths record stampedTrailer's first non-inherited final-block ID, while the amend keep path (line 855) records the last live one.
findings.short_summary: Keep paths record first vs last ID in the stamp marker
findings.failure_scenario: A -F or template message whose final block holds two non-inherited trailers X, Y: the marker records X. On an amend of the same shape it records Y. If the user then moves one out of the final block, post-commit rescues X in one flow and Y in the other, and pickCondensationTarget's 'last without a checkpoint' rule may pick a different target than the user's intent.

findings.summary: hasUserContent (and preparedFinalTrailers) cut at a scissors line even in a message git does not open, but git cuts only under -v or commit.cleanup=scissors.
findings.short_summary: Scissors cut applied to messages git keeps whole
findings.failure_scenario: `git commit -F saved.txt` where saved.txt is a saved `commit -v` message with its scissors line and diff. Git (no editor, whitespace cleanup) records the diff in the message. Prepare judges the trailer above the scissors line as stamped, but the recorded final block is the diff, so attach and explain see the commit as unlinked. If the content sits only below the scissors line, commit-msg strips the trailer of a message git records non-empty.

entries.name: mcp__ccd_session__start_session
entries.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so); the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now. "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), one working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one.

repository.description: With target "cloud", only when the user named a repository other than this project's: "owner/name" on github.com, which the cloud session clones at its default branch. Take the exact owner/name from the user's words or a listing that shows it; if you are not sure of it, ask them. A bypass or auto permission mode may not carry over: the session then starts in the cloud's default mode. If the call is refused, do not run or propose the other repository's work in this project.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

input.title: Real-git matrix test for checkpoint trailer placement
input.name: trailer-git-matrix
input.background: entireio/cli PR #2253 (branch fix-checkpoint-trailer-block, local tip caeefbea7, not pushed) makes only a commit's final git trailer block authorize checkpoint writes. That made trailer placement a correctness problem: each review round found a git commit mode where Entire's prepare-commit-msg left the Entire-Checkpoint trailer outside the final block. The hooks now read git's GIT_EDITOR=: signal (githooks(5): set when git won't open the editor; verified on git 2.50 for -m, --no-edit, -C), locate git's comment block as the trailing comment run after a blank line or the scissors line, and read core.commentChar=auto back from that block. Every existing test simulates git: synthetic messages (gitCommentBlock, gitVerboseTail in cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/checkpoint_trailer_authority_test.go), go-git commits, and hand-set GIT_EDITOR. So the tests share the implementation's assumptions. Known open findings from review: a user-exported GIT_EDITOR=: makes an empty editor commit record a trailer-only commit; and under auto, prepare reads the final block with git's cleanup prefix while post-commit reads it as '#', which can duplicate a trailer on amend.
input.prompt:
Add an integration test (new file under cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/, build tag integration) that drives REAL `git commit` with Entire's hooks installed and pointing at the test-built binary (not the Homebrew `entire` on PATH; see how existing integration tests install hooks and isolate env, and use testutil.GitIsolatedEnv / execx.NonInteractive). Script the editor with a GIT_EDITOR program that applies a per-case edit (leave untouched, type a subject, clear the message, type a body below the trailer).

Matrix:
- Modes: -m; -m -e; plain editor; -v; --amend; --amend --no-edit; -C HEAD; -t template.
- Configs: default; core.commentChar=';'; core.commentChar=auto; commit.status=false; commit.cleanup=strip, whitespace, scissors.
- Message shapes: plain subject; a subject starting with '#'; a body ending in a '#' paragraph; 'Fixes:\n#123'.
Each case needs an agent session with pending work, so prepare stamps a trailer (reuse the authorityAgentTurn-style setup).

Assert three invariants on the recorded commit:
1. Its final trailer block names exactly the stamped checkpoint ID, read with strategy.FinalCheckpointTrailers semantics, and post-commit stored that checkpoint.
2. The user's own lines are unchanged and in their original order.
3. A cleared message aborts the commit and leaves no trailer-only commit.

Use t.Parallel per the repo's test-safety rules and keep the run under a couple of minutes; prune the matrix to representative cells if needed and say which were pruned. Do NOT change production code: when cells fail, mark them t.Skip with a note, or list them, and report the failing cells (mode × config × shape, expected vs got) in your final message. Done = the test file plus a passing run of the cells that hold, and a table of the cells that fail. Run `mise run lint` on the result and commit on your own branch only; do not push.

This case is pretty contrived though, since it would require the user manually reusing a saved commit message file containing their own trailer. I'm now realizing that fixing finding 2 by switching prepare's grammar to match post-commit's "#" rule wouldn't actually resolve the separate whitespace-under-auto issue, since that one affects placement, not just keep decisions—so these are two distinct problems that need separate fixes.

With scissors cleanup plus FROM_COMMIT, git's entire comment block ends up below the cut line, so it's discarded and the trailer placement above the scissors line is actually fine. But for whitespace/verbatim modes, git's hint-plus-status block stays in the kept content, meaning the trailer has to go after that block whenever the grammar can't skip it — and I also need to account for cases where the cleanup prefix comment sits between user content and the trailer.

So the fix is: in the trailer-insertion functions, check whether the comment block will be kept or stripped by the grammar, and only append the trailer after the block when it won't be auto-skipped — essentially when `!rules.stripped && rules.prefix != grammarPrefix`. For the default "#" grammar, the prefix matches so the trailer stays above and the kept block gets skipped correctly by the grammar already.

But I realize this interacts with git's own emptiness/whitespace-cleanup logic: with edited=true and whitespace cleanup, comment lines still count as content for the "untouched message" check, so git ends up recording the comment block plus the trailer anyway — which is actually consistent with how git behaves without Entire's involvement at all.

I'm also reconsidering whether finding 2's fix still makes sense given that real git didn't reproduce it — but the underlying principle holds: prepare's judgment about whether a commit is linked must match whatever grammar the reader (post-commit/attach) actually uses, since auto mode writes trailers with the "#" prefix that the reader expects. Good, the second finding reproduced with real git confirms the trailer duplication bug. Now I'm implementing the fix by adding a grammar field to comment rules, where the configured prefix (or auto-detected "#") gets set during message comment rule setup, and the recorded comment prefix logic uses this to parse trailers correctly.

The key piece is a trailerPrefix helper that resolves "auto" to git's default comment prefix since only `git commit` resolves that itself, while `git interpret-trailers` needs the literal default. Then preparedFinalTrailers needs updating to cut at scissors using the plain prefix but parse trailers using the resolved grammar prefix, with the struct renamed to commentRules holding prefix, trailerPrefix, edited, and stripped fields.

The `-F` test confirms finding 2 via real git, with a second trailer being added. Next I'll apply the root fix: have cuts/strips use git's cleanup prefix while reading the final block with the prefix post-commit actually uses.

content.thinking:
I'm checking edge cases for the trailer logic: when there's no scissors line it falls back to -1 and appends correctly after git's block, and when there's no comment block at all, it also safely returns -1 and appends.

For scissors cleanup with a non-# prefix, git's block starts right at the scissors line itself, so nothing above it counts as "kept." That means keepsBlockAfterTrailer evaluates true and the editor flow skips adding the explanation — a subtle behavior change from before for auto+scissors mode, though it's consistent since scissors mode preserves comment lines regardless of prefix.

I'm reconsidering the right condition: the real test should be whether the trailer placement equals the start of git's comment block, which would require passing the message lines into that decision function rather than relying on prefix rules alone. Refactoring toward a helper that determines whether the trailer follows the block based on both the parsed lines and the rules...

Finishing the helper logic...

I'm weighing whether handling this scissors-mode edge case is worth the complexity -- it's a correctness fix for a narrow corner case (auto mode plus scissors cleanup plus a comment-prefixed line), but it still seems worth including.

I also need to think about the running check: since it's compiling against the current source, modifying files mid-run could cause inconsistent results. I think it's safer to just kill the check now and restart it after making the refinement, rather than waiting for it to finish.

I noticed that with `commit.cleanup=scissors`, git's block gets cut off entirely above the scissors line, but my condition still drops the explanation in that case. I'm stopping the current run, fixing the condition so the explanation survives when git's block is fully cut, then rerunning.

input.title: Extend the real-git trailer test to more modes
input.name: trailer-git-matrix
input.background: entireio/cli PR #2253 (branch fix-checkpoint-trailer-block, local commit dcb6f5633, not yet pushed) makes only a commit's final git trailer block authorize checkpoint writes, so where Entire's prepare-commit-msg places its Entire-Checkpoint trailer is a correctness requirement in every git commit mode. The branch now has TestTrailerAuthority_RealGitCommits (cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/checkpoint_trailer_real_git_test.go). It runs 15 representative real `git commit` cases through gitWithEntireCommitHooksEnv (redo_commit_index_test.go), with Entire's prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit and post-rewrite hooks and a scripted GIT_EDITOR. It asserts that the commit carries exactly one trailer, which is its final block and is stored by post-commit, that the user's lines stay first, and that an untouched editor commit aborts. The hooks rely on git setting GIT_EDITOR=: when it opens no editor, on git's comment block being the trailing comment run after a blank line or the scissors line, and on core.commentChar=auto being read back from that block. Known documented limits: a user-exported GIT_EDITOR=: is indistinguishable from git's signal; explain's history listings still use the first ID anywhere.
input.prompt: After PR #2253 merges (or on top of its branch if it has not), extend TestTrailerAuthority_RealGitCommits toward the full matrix: modes -m, -m -e, editor, -v, --amend, --amend --no-edit, -C, -c, -t template, --fixup=amend:, --squash; configs default, core.commentChar ';' and a multi-character core.commentString, auto, commit.status=false, commit.cleanup strip/whitespace/scissors/verbatim, plus a non-English LANG for git's hint text; message shapes: plain, '#' subject, body ending in a '#' paragraph, 'Fixes:\n#123', a template with its own comment prompts, a Signed-off-by from -s. > A commit whose stamped trailer the user moves out of the final block in the editor, for example by typing a body below it, is still condensed into that checkpoint: post-commit accepts the trailer prepare left. Attach and `explain --generate` read only the final block, so they treat that commit as unlinked, and `--generate` names the out-of-block checkpoint in its error. Moving the trailer back would take a new step in commit-msg, so it is left out.
>

>
> `explain`'s history listings still match a commit by the first checkpoint ID in its message.

That commit adds TestTrailerAuthority_RealGitCommits (cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/checkpoint_trailer_real_git_test.go): 15 real `git commit` cases run through gitWithEntireCommitHooksEnv (redo_commit_index_test.go), which installs Entire's prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit and post-rewrite hooks and takes a scripted GIT_EDITOR. Each case asserts that the commit carries exactly one trailer, that it is the final block and post-commit stored it, that the user's lines stay first, and that an untouched editor commit aborts. The hooks rely on three things: git setting GIT_EDITOR=: when it opens no editor; git's comment block being the trailing comment run after a blank line, or the scissors line; and core.commentChar=auto being read back from that block. Prepare reads the final block with post-commit's trailer grammar (auto reads as '#'). Under auto with a cleanup that keeps comments, the trailer goes after git's kept block. Documented limits: a user-exported GIT_EDITOR=: is indistinguishable from git's signal; explain's history listings still use the first ID anywhere.

In entireio/cli the quality bar is *evidence*, not code volume. Stefan Haubold (`Soph`) wrote 25 of the last 60 commits as of 2026-08-14 and sets the house style. Diffs are often tiny (#1985 was +6/-1); PR bodies are lab notebooks.

The beat order every exemplar PR follows: **Problem** (failure quoted verbatim, real log/CI output) → **Cause** (traced to a specific commit, often by diffing logs from the last green run) → **Fix** (framed as removing an asymmetry, reusing an existing helper, not adding a mechanism) → **Why nothing caught it** (explicit coverage-gap post-mortem) → **Tests, "Verified RED"** (named tests plus the exact pre-fix failure message) → **Rejected alternatives** (with cost, e.g. "~4 signatures and ~45 call sites") → **Test plan checkboxes** ending in `mise run check`.

Two habits worth copying: performance claims use **interleaved** A/B runs with medians (sequential runs let the first arm absorb cold page-cache cost and invert the result — stated in both #1985 and #1968), and negative/deflated results get reported honestly (#1985 talked itself down from a 49% headline to 2%).

**Why:** matching this format is the highest-leverage thing for getting contributions merged fast, and it is doable before deep Go fluency.
**How to apply:** write the failing test first so its real output becomes the "Verified RED" line — the test discipline and the PR-body discipline are the same act. Full playbook artifact: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0228a8ac-84b6-413e-bd05-5621d7dfb4f3 . See [[entire-1927-contribution-thread]].
Fixes #2255
Fixes #2256

An `Entire-Checkpoint:` line anywhere in a commit message still decides which checkpoint a commit writes to. Main's provenance check (`stampedByAnotherCommit`) only refuses a checkpoint that already exists in the local store, so a checkpoint ID in a commit body, whether pasted, quoted, indented, or mentioned mid-sentence, still steers three writes.

This PR now also carries #2259 (the trailer writer fix). The stricter reader here is what makes that writer bug reachable, so the two need to land together, and I'm closing #2259 in favour of this one.

## Problem

I ported the scenarios onto current main and ran them there:

| Scenario on main | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `entire attach` on a commit whose body says `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` | The attached session is written into `<id>`, which ends up holding two unrelated sessions. Same for an indented line and for "Follow-up to Entire-Checkpoint: <id> from last week." |
| `git commit -m` with that line in the body, `<id>` not in this clone | prepare-commit-msg treats it as already stamped and adds no trailer. Post-commit then condenses the session's work under `<id>`, claiming an ID that may belong to a teammate's unfetched checkpoint. |
| Same, `<id>` already in this clone | Post-commit correctly refuses to write there, but the commit ends up with no checkpoint at all. |
| `entire explain --commit <sha> --generate` | Resolves the first mention anywhere in the message. |

## Cause

Every place that decides "may I write to this checkpoint" reads trailers with `ParseCheckpoint`/`ParseAllCheckpoints`, whose regex is unanchored and scans the whole message. That is right for discovery, since squash commits carry their squashed commits' trailers in the body, and wrong for deciding a write.

## Fix

Only the final trailer block, read by git's grammar, decides a write:

- `stampedTrailer` (prepare-commit-msg and the agent fast path) and `stampedTrailersOf` (post-commit)
- the amend handler, which still treats a deleted ID mentioned anywhere as stripped, as main does
- attach's `planAttachLink` and `resolveCheckpointID`, switched together so joining and resolving agree
- explain's `--generate` paths; read-only explain keeps whole-message discovery

Prepare reads the message as git will record it (`trailers.StripEditorComments`): an editor message loses the lines starting with git's comment prefix and everything from the exact scissors line down, while a `-m`/`-F` message keeps every line as content. The prefix is `core.commentChar` or `core.commentString` (aliases, last one set wins), `#` when unset, and for `auto` it is read back from the comment block git wrote. Prepare writes its explanation and inherited trailers with the same prefix, so git's cleanup removes the explanation. Trailer lines accept `Key:value` and tab separators, as git does. The final-block reader rejects leading-whitespace pseudo-trailers, accepts indented lines only as continuations, never reads the subject paragraph as trailers, and skips lines starting with git's comment prefix, as git's trailer parser does. That last part matters because `commit.cleanup=scissors` and `whitespace` keep comment lines, so the recorded commit carries Entire's explanation right below its trailer. Post-commit, attach and `explain --generate` read a recorded commit with the configured prefix (`auto` reads as `#`, as in `git interpret-trailers`), and only look the prefix up when the message names a checkpoint that a read without it misses. The writer from #2259 joins only a trailer block without comment lines, so a trailer it appends is always one the readers accept.

Every trailer prepare adds to an editor message goes above the comment block that ends it, whether it is the template's, an amend's restored or fresh one, an agent's, or an inherited one, so `commit -v` cannot cut it off. The template puts prepare's explanation in its own paragraph between the user's lines and the trailer: a subject typed on the line just above cannot join the trailer into the subject paragraph, and cleanup modes that keep comments leave the trailer as its own block. Like git, the reader also accepts a block holding a `Signed-off-by:` or `(cherry picked from commit …)` line with other lines in it, while trailers make up at least a quarter of the block. `explain --generate` writes into the block's last ID, the one attach joins.

The commit-msg hook's empty-message check now counts content the way git's cleanup will. git does not tell commit-msg how the message was written, but an editor message ends with git's comment block or carries prepare's explanation, and a `-m`/`-F` message has neither, so prefix lines count as comments only in an editor message, using the same comment prefix and exact scissors line. Under `commit.cleanup=strip`, which git applies to `-m` messages too, they count as comments in every message. Before, an untouched editor message with `core.commentChar=;` or `commit -v` was committed holding only the trailer instead of aborting, and `git commit -m "#42 fix login"` lost its trailer; both also happen on main.

Unchanged on purpose: read-only lookups (resume, status, attribution, read-only explain), squash and redo inheritance, and `RemoveCheckpointTrailers`, which stays broad so a delete removes every copy.

## Why nothing caught it

Main already stops a leftover mention of a deleted checkpoint from counting as the commit's own (`TestCheckpointDelete_LeftoverDeletedIDNeverReceivesNewWork`), by filtering through the deleted list. The same leftover naming a live or unfetched checkpoint was not covered, and attach and explain had no test with a body mention at all.

## Tests, verified RED before the fix

Each failed on main's call sites (I merged main first) and passes now:

- **Body mentions:** `checkpoint_trailer_authority_test.go` (real hook binaries), `TestAttach_*DoesNotSelectCheckpoint` and `TestExplainGenerate_BodyCheckpointLineIsNotATrailer`. A pasted, indented or prose `Entire-Checkpoint:` line is no longer reused by prepare, joined by attach, or written by `explain --generate`.
- **Comment prefix and scissors:** `EditorCommitHonorsCommentChar`, `AmendHonorsCommentChar`, `ProseScissorsMarkerIsNotACut`, `UntouchedEditorMessageAborts` and `MessageSubjectStartingWithHashKeepsTrailer`. `;`, `auto`, `commit -v` and `-m "#42 …"` messages are read the way git cleans them.
- **Cleanup modes that keep comments:** `CleanupKeepingCommentsLinksTheCommit` and `TestAttach_TrailerFollowedByCommentLinesJoinsCheckpoint`. With `commit.cleanup=scissors` or `whitespace` the trailer still links the commit, as `git interpret-trailers` reads it.
- **Grammar:** `trailers_test.go` covers the subject paragraph, continuations, `Key:value` and tab separators, and comment lines.

`VerboseAmendKeepsItsTrailer` and `TestExplainReadOnly_FindsBodyCheckpointLine` are guards that pass before and after.

Review then found regressions in the stricter rule itself; these failed on the branch before their fix:

- **Trailers prepare adds:** `AddedTrailerSurvivesVerboseCleanup` (amend restore, amend after a delete, agent editor commit), `ClearedAmendMessageAborts`, `SubjectOnTheTemplatesSecondLineLinks`, the `auto` row of `CleanupKeepingCommentsLinksTheCommit`, and the `AnchorsToTheEndingBlock` unit tests. `UntouchedEditorMessageAborts` gains a `commit.status=false` guard.
- **Git's block rule and explain:** the cherry-pick and quarter-trailer cases in `trailers_test.go`, and `TestExplainGenerate_UsesTheLastFinalBlockTrailer`.
- **`commit.cleanup=strip` and scissors:** `StripCleanupMessageOfCommentsAborts`, and the CRLF scissors case in `trailers_test.go`, where git does not cut.

## Rejected alternatives

- Anchoring the whole-message regex to line starts: a body line could still steer writes, and indented squash messages would stop being discovered.
- Checking only that the named checkpoint exists: existence says nothing about whether this commit stamped it, and it misses IDs this clone has not fetched.
- Guessing `auto` from the whole message: once git has written its comment block, the character it chose always looks used, so the guess is wrong. The prefix is read back from git's own block instead.

## Known gap

A commit whose stamped trailer the user moves out of the final block in the editor, for example by typing a body below it, is still condensed into that checkpoint: post-commit accepts the trailer prepare left. Attach and `explain --generate` read only the final block, so they treat that commit as unlinked, and `--generate` names the out-of-block checkpoint in its error. Moving the trailer back would take a new step in commit-msg, so it is left out.

The hooks read git's `GIT_EDITOR=:` as "no editor". A `GIT_EDITOR=:` you export yourself looks the same, so such a commit gets its trailer after git's comment block (lost with `-v`), and a message saved untouched is recorded holding only the trailer instead of aborting.

`explain`'s history listings still match a commit by the first checkpoint ID in its message.

Squash and redo inheritance still scan the whole message of the squashed or reset commits, so an `Entire-Checkpoint:` mention in one of their bodies is carried into the new commit's final trailer block. Fixing it needs per-commit parsing of SQUASH_MSG and a rule for nested squashes, so it is left for a follow-up.

A GitHub "Squash and merge" commit joins the squashed messages without indentation, so its final block is the last squashed commit's trailer and attach joins that checkpoint, as on main. Telling it apart needs a way to recognize squash merges.

## Branch history

This branch predates main's provenance model. I merged current main, resolved every call-site conflict to main's version (the legacy migration this PR used to touch is gone), and re-applied the final-block reads to main's call sites in the last commit. The diff against main is the change to review.

## Test plan

- [x] `mise run check`: fmt, lint and all CI tests pass, except two load timeouts (hook-chain install, external agent discovery) that pass alone and are untouched here
- [x] real `git commit` with `core.commentChar` unset, `;`, `//` and `auto`, fresh and amend, including the commit-msg abort cases
- [x] CI

Unchanged on purpose: read-only lookups (resume, status, attribution, read-only explain), squash and redo inheritance, and `RemoveCheckpointTrailers`, which stays broad so a delete removes every copy.

## Why nothing caught it

Main already stops a leftover mention of a deleted checkpoint from counting as the commit's own (`TestCheckpointDelete_LeftoverDeletedIDNeverReceivesNewWork`), by filtering through the deleted list. The same leftover naming a live or unfetched checkpoint was not covered, and attach and explain had no test with a body mention at all.
